qt: to the Commission Jordi Solé (Verts/ALE) Subject:

In Spain it is mandatory for all lawyers practising in that Member State to provide pro bono legal assistance (Article 1 of Law 1/1996). This also applies to solicitors. The mandatory nature of this pro bono legal assistance became particularly apparent recently, as all lawyers in certain judicial districts deregisterd from the service in protest against abismal pay and unjustified payment delays of almost half a year. In response, professional associations have resorted to forcing lawyers to register to provide pro bono legal assistance, imposing work on them in accordance with this law. Lawyers are somewhat limited in their ability to negotiate salary increases, especially in the light of the various unappealable court rulings that have become final and which prohibit unionisation and collective bargaining. Does the Commission consider that imposing a mandatory service onto all members of a profession is at odds with Article 5 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, as well as the directives that govern unjustified discriminatory practices on grounds of employment status?
at: (English version) to the Commission Jordi Solé (Verts/ALE) (17 April 2024) Subject: Requirement for all lawyers to provide pro bono legal assistance In Spain it is mandatory for all lawyers practising in that Member State to provide pro bono legal assistance (Article 1 of Law 1/1996). (12 June 2024) Under Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU (1) (the Charter) everyone whose rights guaranteed by EU law are violated has the right to an effective remedy and to a fair trial, including the right to legal aid for those who lack sufficient resources. In line with Article 51(1) thereof, an individual may rely on Article 47 in the context of proceedings before national courts if these are related to the alleged violation, application or implementation of EU law. When applicable, Article 47 leaves to the Member States a free choice of the means to be used in guaranteeing legal aid, in so far as such aid is necessary to ensure effective access to justice. Regarding the alleged violation of Article 5 of the Charter, where the Charter is applicable, it does not appear on the basis of the information provided by the Honourable Member that the situation described would amount to such a violation (2). On the issue of the delayed payment to lawyers from the national legal aid scheme, the Commission would like to stress that Article 4 of the Late Payment Directive (3) provides that, concerning transactions between providers and public authorities, public authorities have to pay for the goods and services that they procure within 30 days or, in very exceptional circumstances, within 60 days. This directive has been implemented in all the Member States.
